content: 1. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of home modifications for individuals with low vision, focusing on accessibility as outlined in the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. The review utilized the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) version 2011 to assess the quality of included studies. 2. Two quasi-experimental studies (Fänge 2005, Petersson 2008) involving 245 participants in Sweden examined the impact of home modifications on activities of daily living (ADL) dependence. The studies included 131 adults over 18 years with functional limitations and 114 adults over 40 years with everyday life challenges. The interventions were not found to significantly reduce participants' dependence. The quality of evidence was rated as low. 3. Four studies (Gitlin 2006, Petersson 2008, Petersson 2009, Stineman 2007) assessed difficulties in ADL and institutional ADL. These included one randomized trial (Gitlin 2006), two quasi-experimental studies (Petersson 2008, 2009), and one cross-sectional study (Stineman 2007). The studies involved 319 adults over 70 years in the USA, 114 and 103 adults over 40 years in Sweden, and 25,805 adults over 18 years with disabilities in the USA. The evidence was inconsistent and imprecise, with low quality. 4. One quasi-experimental study (Petersson 2008) involving 114 adults over 40 years in Sweden evaluated the impact of home modifications on safety in ADL. The study found moderate evidence of direct and precise effects, but the quality of evidence was low. 5. A randomized trial (Gitlin 2006) involving 319 adults over 70 years in the USA assessed self-efficacy in ADL. The study found moderate evidence of direct and precise effects, but the quality of evidence was low. 6. A randomized trial (Brunnström 2004) involving 46 adults with low vision in Sweden evaluated certainty in performing specific ADL tasks. The study found no significant changes in perceived activity performance in the kitchen and bathroom after six months. The quality of evidence was low. 7. Three studies (Edgren 2015, Slaug 2017, Tongsiri 2017) assessed general ADL performance. These included one randomized trial (Edgren 2015), one quasi-experimental study (Tongsiri 2017), and one cross-sectional study (Slaug 2017). The studies involved 81 adults over 60 years in Finland, 43 individuals with physical disabilities in Thailand, and 636 adults aged 80-89 years in Sweden and Germany. The evidence was inconsistent, with moderate quality. 8. Four studies (Ahmad 2013, Brunnström 2004, Gitlin 2014, Tongsiri 2017) evaluated quality of life or well-being. These included two randomized trials (Ahmad 2013, Brunnström 2004), one quasi-experimental study (Tongsiri 2017), and one cross-sectional study (Gitlin 2014). The studies involved 40 wheelchair users in Pakistan, 46 adults with low vision in Sweden, 43 individuals with physical disabilities in Thailand, and 88 dyads of adults with dementia and their caregivers in the USA. Home modifications and lighting improvements were associated with significant improvements in quality of life in some studies, but the overall evidence was low. 9. Four studies (Campbell 2005, Carlsson 2017, Maggi 2018, Tchalla 2012) assessed falls or injuries. These included one randomized trial (Campbell 2005), two quasi-experimental studies (Carlsson 2017, Maggi 2018), and one cohort study (Tchalla 2012). The studies involved 391 adults over 75 years with severe visual impairment in New Zealand, 143 adults in Sweden, 1565 frail adults over 65 years in Belgium, and 194 frail adults over 65 years in France. The evidence was moderate and consistent. 10. One randomized trial (Gitlin 2006/2009) involving 319 adults over 70 years in the USA assessed mortality. The study found no significant differences in mortality at three years. The quality of evidence was low. 11. One quasi-experimental study (Stark 2004) involving 29 low-income adults aged 57-82 years in the USA evaluated occupational performance. The study found significant improvements in occupational performance after six months. The quality of evidence was high. 12. One cross-sectional study (Norin 2017) involving 123 adults in Sweden assessed participation. Accessibility problems were significantly associated with reduced participation and autonomy. The quality of evidence was very low.
